content: Asthma is a chronic respiratory condition affecting approximately 300 million individuals globally, contributing significantly to both morbidity and mortality. Omalizumab, a monoclonal antibody, functions by binding to and neutralizing free serum immunoglobulin E (IgE), a key immune mediator implicated in the pathophysiology of asthma. This drug, classified as an anti-IgE therapy, has been recommended by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) since 2013 as an add-on treatment for individuals aged six years and older with severe, persistent, allergic, IgE-mediated asthma that remains inadequately controlled despite frequent or continuous oral corticosteroid use. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of omalizumab compared to placebo or conventional asthma therapies in both adults and children. A systematic search of relevant studies was conducted, with the most recent search completed in June 2013. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving anti-IgE therapy, regardless of administration route or duration, were included, provided that co-interventions were consistent across study arms. The review focused on subcutaneous administration, as this is the route predominantly used in clinical practice. A total of 25 trials were included in the analysis, with 11 new studies added since the previous review. Of these, 19 trials specifically evaluated the efficacy of subcutaneous omalizumab as an adjunct to corticosteroid therapy. Among participants with moderate to severe asthma who were receiving background inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) therapy, subcutaneous omalizumab significantly reduced the likelihood of asthma exacerbations compared to placebo (odds ratio [OR] 0.55, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.42 to 0.60). This corresponds to an absolute reduction in exacerbation rates from 26% in the placebo group to 16% in the omalizumab group over a treatment period of 16 to 60 weeks. Hospitalization rates were also significantly lower in participants treated with subcutaneous omalizumab compared to placebo (OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.42), with an absolute risk reduction from 3% in the placebo group to 0.5% in the omalizumab group over 28 to 60 weeks. However, data on hospitalizations were not separately reported for the severe asthma subgroup, and these findings pertain to participants with moderate to severe asthma. Participants receiving subcutaneous omalizumab were more likely to completely discontinue ICS therapy compared to those on placebo (OR 2.50, 95% CI 2.00 to 3.13). Additionally, a modest but statistically significant reduction in daily ICS dose was observed in the omalizumab group (weighted mean difference [WMD] -118 mcg beclomethasone dipropionate [BDP] equivalent per day, 95% CI -154 to -84). However, no significant difference was found between omalizumab and placebo groups in the proportion of participants able to discontinue oral corticosteroid (OCS) therapy (OR 1.18, 95% CI 0.53 to 2.63). Omalizumab treatment was associated with a small but significant reduction in the use of rescue beta2-agonist medication compared to placebo (mean difference [MD] -0.39 puffs per day, 95% CI -0.55 to -0.24). This benefit was observed in both moderate to severe asthma (MD -0.58, 95% CI -0.84 to -0.31) and severe asthma (MD -0.30, 95% CI -0.49 to -0.10) subgroups receiving background ICS therapy. However, no significant difference in rescue medication use was noted in participants with severe asthma who were on both inhaled and oral corticosteroids. Fewer serious adverse events were reported in participants treated with subcutaneous omalizumab compared to placebo (OR 0.72, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.91). However, injection site reactions were more common in the omalizumab group, increasing from 5.6% with placebo to 9.1% with omalizumab. In conclusion, subcutaneous omalizumab demonstrated efficacy in reducing asthma exacerbations and hospitalizations when used as an adjunct to inhaled corticosteroids or during steroid tapering. It also facilitated reductions in ICS use and was generally well tolerated, although injection site reactions were more frequent. Further research is needed to evaluate its effects in pediatric populations, to explore its potential prednisolone-sparing effects, and to identify biomarkers predictive of treatment response. Additionally, the optimal baseline serum IgE level for achieving maximum efficacy remains unclear, and given the high cost of omalizumab, identifying patients most likely to benefit is a priority for future investigations.
